Hi guys
I want to share a method that made me over $3,000 in a single day.
When using
https://swapzone.io
(a crypto exchange aggregator) to swap Bitcoin into another cryptocurrency, there's a way to boost your payout by around 37% due to a miscalculation on one of their partner exchange offers - ChangeNOW.
For example, swapping $2000 worth of BTC can return $2740 worth of any other coin, instantly locking in a ~$740 profit.
The trick is to force Swapzone to route the ChangeNOW offer through their older backend node (version 1.9), which is still connected to the aggregator but no longer used on ChangeNOW's main website. This older node calculates BTC to ANY conversion using an outdated formula that inflates the payout.
📌 Full instructions for loading the node are here:
https://docs.google.com/document/d/1Nk_c...sp=sharing
⚠️ Tips:
Keep each transaction below 0.05 BTC to avoid triggering KYC (anything above that could result in your funds being held).

We managed to access the Company_Bus folder, which contains a treasure trove of sensitive data, including business agreements, employee agreements, employment contracts, contracts and agreements, company budgets and financial reports, payment receipts, invoices, and all financial and accounting data. We also obtained HR forms, leave requests, payroll records, and complete employee data.
Most importantly, we extracted official government forms from the Sultanate of Brunei Darussalam, foreign work permits, and highly sensitive government data. We also obtained the complete Goldunited system credentials and the company's IP address list from the IP List.xlsx file, in addition to detailed technical and network data.
We also obtained complete identity documents belonging to an employee, Sultan Anta Azaoudin, born on September 19, 1996, in Tulungagung, Indonesia, who holds passport number C7801153, issued on March 31, 2022, and expiring on March 31, 2027. This means that we possess his complete passport details and can use them for identity theft operations.
In addition, we extracted a list of foreign workers authorized to work for the company, with various nationalities such as Indonesian, Indian, Bangladeshi, Malaysian, and Pakistani. All this data includes their full names, dates of birth, passport numbers, salaries, and work permit expiration dates.

Swedish tire and rubber-repair shop database

Each location uses its own point-of-sale system, either Compilator or Eontyre. Customer, order, invoice, and tire storage data is collected from these systems and stored in a central Postgres database. The data is then cleaned and organized into tables and KPI views that cover orders, revenue, tire storage usage, and customer data quality.

About the leak
American insurance giant Allstate's staging CRM — a Firebase-powered tax preparation, client management, and Stripe billing platform left completely open to the public internet. Firebase Realtime Database
allstate-staging.firebaseio.com
— no auth, no token, no referer check. Full read AND write. Anyone who knows the URL can dump the entire database AND inject data. Write escalation confirmed on 5/5 test operations — admin user created, business account injected, transaction modified, all HTTP 200.
The database contains 968 Stripe transactions across 20 unique production customer IDs, 7 business accounts with real tax IDs and incorporation documents, 11 user profiles with Social Security Numbers, employee pay periods with hours logged, and 9 SMS conversations between agents and clients exchanging tax return documents via Firebase Storage download links. The admin's session JWT tokens are sitting in plaintext in the user profile —
securetoken.google.com
issuer with full idToken strings. Six Firebase Storage download tokens were extracted from conversation attachments, exposing uploaded client documents.
This is a staging environment that somehow has 968 real Stripe production invoices and SSNs for real people. The customer ID prefix confirms these are live-mode Stripe customer objects — not test-mode placeholders. Allstate's staging CRM is a Stripe production billing platform with open read/write to the world.

This isn't a sophisticated exploit. This is a Firebase Realtime Database with the security rules set to
".read": true, ".write": true
— the equivalent of leaving your database password in a README.md committed to a public repo. Google sends automated "your database is insecure" warnings to the Firebase project owner. For years. group: What are the best platforms to learn offensive security (free) - RaidForums
text:
TryHackMe and HackTheBox are two of the more popular above-board ones. HackTheBox also has a thread somewhere in here with captured flags (but if you're tryna learn, you shouldn't cheat that way anyways). Both are somewhat freemium. They have paid plans, but a lot of the material is free.
Beyond that, it really just depends what you wanna do. Without specifics, not much guidance can be given. Learning paths for web app targets is going to be very different than learning maldev which is going to be very different than learning reveng etc

There was a line "Status: partial" in your original post, yes. But 1 word means very little (partial fields? partial download? there is more available for sale?). The forum rules state "You must specify the amount of users."
And it still doesn't explain how the customer list (with 670 users) has emails like "barbg60@juno,com", "propermom@yahoo.co,m", "11`23", "TEST", "a", "aaa@bbb.com", and many appearing 3-4 times each.
This is not a list of people who placed orders with the company. With so many fake email/address, it would be impossible for them to ship those orders.
I will add this: the OP did just send me evidence that this did come from a server, and was not some old file being passed around like I originally thought.

group: NVIDIAScape: OCI Hook Inheritance Flaws in AI Infra - RaidForums
text:
Taking a look at NVIDIAScape after its Pwn2Own reveal. CDI mode allows env vars like LD_PRELOAD to propagate through OCI hooks, inverting isolation for root execution on the host. More or less under-discussed aspect in shared AI clusters, this opens vectors for model exfiltration or poisoning, especially via tainted Hugging Face images in supply chains. Reminds me of older runc vulnerabilities, but the GPU element part takes it to another level, this vulnerability hitting roughly 37% of cloud AI services. I also found this a bit amateur like, because this is mostly privilege escalation for babies, and this coming from a very trusted company.
I wont bother writing a exploit since anyone with a brain can figure out how to abuse this.
Not sure if anyone else will find this interesting, but i did.

They’re “split” because they come from different teams with different goals and security philosophies. Yes, CalyxOS is strong enough for daily use—but GrapheneOS is objectively stricter and more hardened.
1) Why GrapheneOS and CalyxOS are separate projects
They are not forks of each other in a simple way. They diverged because of
ideology + technical direction
.
GrapheneOS philosophy
Focus:
maximum security + minimal attack surface
Key points:
No Google Play by default (optional sandboxed Play Services)
Strong memory hardening, exploit mitigations, SELinux tuning
Very strict security model
Minimal convenience features if they weaken security
Pixel-only devices (for hardware security reasons)
Think of it as:
“Security first, even if usability suffers.”
CalyxOS philosophy
Focus:
privacy + usability balance
Key points:
MicroG included by default (Google compatibility without Google)
Easier app compatibility
More user-friendly defaults
Less aggressive hardening than GrapheneOS
Supports more devices (not only Pixel)
Think of it as:
“Privacy-friendly Android that normal people can use daily.”
2) Is CalyxOS strong enough for everyday use?
Yes — for most people.
CalyxOS is:
More private than stock Android
More secure than typical custom ROMs
Stable enough for daily driver
Compatible with banking apps, social apps, etc.

Hardened malloc / memory allocator

Per-app network + sensor toggles
Better sandboxing of Google Play
Attack surface reduction
CalyxOS adds:

Tor / VPN friendly defaults
Less strict SELinux policies
Important truth:
MicroG = convenience gain, security loss (relative to GrapheneOS).

Choose GrapheneOS if:
You care about OPSEC, malware, zero-days

CalyxOS = professional civilian security

text:
We are releasing a preview of the WoundTech breach -- one of the most disturbing medical data exposures we've ever encountered, impacting
160,000+ ID-linked individuals
and close to
a million exposed patients
with other identifiers
, and exposing years of
graphic wound photos, detailed medical records, and doctors' notes, including on mental health, drug addiction, domestic abuse,
and other
extremely sensitive
topics.
The full data set will be added to this post in the coming days.
We've redacted last names and partial other identifying information from these because
we believe in basic human dignity -- something WoundTech clearly doesn't
. Journalists, researchers, and attorneys can reach out to us for full unredacted samples at threatspians@fulcrumsec.net. Email us from your organization's domain -- we are not sending unredacted data to Proton/Onion/Yop Mail accounts.
Also of note is the sheer scale of the data Woundtech's incompetence exposed here. Using their AWS Cloudwatch access, we determined that the full exposure was 3,8 tb of medical records and wound photos alone. We did not exfiltrate all of it  before they rotated AWS credentials within 24 hours of initial access -- something which we applaud them for! But by then it was too late. We had already
exfiltrated nearly a terabyte of pure PII/PHI
, including the
COMPLETE 4.6 MILLION CLINICAL NOTES they kept cavalierly in plain text.
That's the thing about breach severity: once it reaches the level of
CATASTROPHIC
, the degree of catastrophe hardly matters.
We look forward to seeing them try to spin this in the media, trying to explain how "only" 160,000 patients had their entire medical history, their doctor's notes about their conditions, and photographs of their wounds leaked (many of the latter on the buttocks and other private areas). Or to their own patients. Probably through lies and obfuscation -- they're that sort of company.
The fact is,
Woundtech will be forever known as that healthcare company who failed to protect their patients.
Who left a million complete medical records unencrypted in an S3 bucket
, with the keys to access them sitting
plaintext in the env of a vulnerable server
. Their name will be forever synonymous with
FAILURE, DATA BREACH, BREACH OF PRIVACY, and BETRAYAL
of their vulnerable patients.
---
THE INVENTORY
- Total Patients Impacted:
160,000+ individuals
identified by name
, date of birth, medical record number, SSN (about ~25-35%), along with multiple other identifiers and detailed PHI, including referral documents and often COMPLETE MEDICAL RECORDS.
Note: There are close to
a million unique patients in the clinical notes
(see below), but we are only counting the 160,000 that can be cross-referenced and identified by name via the data that we possess.
- Clinical Notes:
4.6 MILLION narrative notes
of doctors and nurses on their patients, documenting the most sensitive medical information imaginable
- S3 EMR Files:
178,885 files:
~85,000 PDF referral documents with full patient PHI and full medical records, some as long as 80+ pages with decades of patient history
~93,000 clinical wound photographs of an extraordinarily graphic nature
- Insurance Records:
5,181,555 capitation records
spanning patients from newborns to 96-year-olds
- Staff Exposed:
2,975 employees/contractors with corporate email addresses and phone numbers
- Production Creds:
Django superuser passwords, database connection strings, Azure AD secrets. Thank you Woundtech, for helping us lateral with ease through your environment!
---
Samples from the clinical notes:
Paul A█████, 39, Male, Blue Shield:
> "History obtained from patient's sister. Patient is a 39 year old male with a history of schizophrenia. Patient has a mobility impairment and spends prolonged periods of time in bed... Barriers to healing: Decreased mobility, incontinence, Schizophrenia, Parkinson. Patient is bed bound, malnutrition (BMI 17.8)."
His full name, DOB (June 28, 1985), Blue Shield subscriber ID, and complete psychiatric history — all cross-referenced in a dataset that was sitting unencrypted on S3.
Fei W███, 63, Male, Anthem Blue Cross:
> "S - Wound on right dorsal foot. Reports that he has injected heroin once since previous visit. Patient is in excruciating pain from self-removing the old dressing. A - Wound type - heroin injection usage"
And from another note on the same patient:
> "Patient has history of injecting himself with heroin and is the reason he developed abscess wounds."
His Anthem Blue Cross subscriber information, his SSN (in his medical record PDF), his doctor's name — linked directly to documentation of his heroin use.
Christina M█████, 25, Female, United Healthcare:
> "Social Hx: Methamphetamine abuse, daily smoker, alcohol abuse. Barriers to healing: Insulin dependent DM2, DM polyneuropathy, history of recurring and current Methamphetamine use, non compliant with follow up with multiple no shows and cancelled appointments."
She's barely 25 years old, and her complete substance abuse history is stored alongside her United Healthcare subscriber ID.
Lawrence H██████, 66, Male, Blue Shield:
> "Barriers to healing: HTN, HLD, ESRD, paraplegia, HIV, lack of social support, substance abuse, poor nutrition"
His HIV status. His full name. His DOB (March 24, 1959). His Blue Shield insurance. All connected. All exposed.
---
When these patients spoke to their healthcare providers about their most personal and private issues and experiences, do you think they expected these confessions to be stored so insecurely a rudimentary hack would allow access to them? Would they have allowed wound care nurses to photograph their heroin injection wounds, bedsore ulcers and diabetic foot wounds?
They never imagined these documents and images would end up in S3 buckets configured with credentials sitting in unencrypted Terraform state files.
Shame on you, Woundtech, for breaking that trust so cavalierly.

A note on redactions:
To avoid re-victimizing the patients that Woundtech has already betrayed, we've redacted surnames and partially redacted patient phone numbers, SSNs, addresses, MRNs, and some other identifying data. We are in the process of partially redacting the entire data set to maintain patient privacy while still fully documenting the breach.
We do this because these patients did nothing wrong. They developed wounds that required professional care. They trusted their healthcare providers to protect their most intimate information. Woundtech doubly betrayed that trust, first when they prioritized speed-to-market over basic security hygiene, and now Woundtech has let them down yet again by refusing to pay a modest fee to protect their private data.
We look forward to watching the upcoming class action lawsuits against this terrible company.
